title: Re'eh: as you were blessed (Deuteronomy 16:17)
hook: each gives according to the blessing they have received

segments.voice: Yesterday, simcha: four of yours and four of God's at the festival table. Your line was rejoice together. Who did you invite? Today, the last verse of Re'eh, about what each guest brings. Day five hundred one.

Every office has done it. Someone's leaving, and an envelope goes around for a gift. Somebody suggests everyone put in twenty dollars. And immediately it's awkward. For the manager, twenty is nothing. For the part-time assistant saving for rent, it's a real bite. A flat amount sounds fair, and isn't. A percentage sounds cold, and is fairer. Nobody quite knows how to say it out loud. The last verse of Re'eh says it out loud, in a handful of words, about pilgrims arriving at the Temple three times a year.
screen: `THE ENVELOPE GOES AROUND.` → `TWENTY DOLLARS, FAIR OR NOT?` → `THE VERSE SAYS IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Three times a year, the chapter says, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, the people go up to the place God chooses. And, in the old Jewish translation: "they shall not appear before the LORD empty." Everyone brings something. But how much? The next verse answers: "Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which He hath given thee." In Hebrew, ish k'matnat yado: each person according to the gift of his hand. No flat fee. No single price. The measure is what you've been given. The Mishnah, in tractate Chagigah, works it out for the festival offerings. Someone with many mouths to feed and little money brings what they can, shaped to their household. Someone with much brings more. Same command, different amounts. Notice the two sides of it. Nobody comes empty. Even the poorest pilgrim brings something, and so stands in the courtyard as a giver, not just a receiver. And nobody hides behind a small number when they've been given a great deal. The verse doesn't shame anyone in either direction. It asks one quiet question: what have you been blessed with? This verse also ends a Torah reading used on the last days of the festivals, and in many synagogues those are days when the memorial prayer, Yizkor, is said, and people pledge gifts in memory of those they've lost. Giving, again, according to what you were given, including the people who gave it.
screen: `NOT EMPTY.` · `K'MATNAT YADO: THE GIFT OF HIS HAND.` · `MANY MOUTHS, LITTLE MONEY.` · `A GIVER, NOT JUST A RECEIVER.` · then, large: `ACCORDING TO YOUR BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give in proportion to what you have. Settle, and breathe. Take honest stock, not just of money. Time. Health. A skill. Free evenings. A car. A calm temperament. Patience with kids. Which of these do you have more of this season than the people around you? Now think of one place to give from that surplus, in proportion. If you have little money but a lot of time, the gift might be time. If you have little time but more money, maybe the reverse. The bell holds the time.
Re'eh. See. The portion that ends with each pilgrim giving according to the blessing they've been given.
Your line: according to your blessing. Today, give one thing you have more of than you need, sized to what you've been given. Day five hundred one.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone should give what they can.
what it means: no one comes empty, no one hides behind a small number; the measure is what you were given.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Chagigah 1:5 scales the festival offerings to a household's means, reading k'matnat yado.
